newsitem.title: Lithuania: Perry letter reassures Balts on NATO future.
newsitem.headline: Perry letter reassures Balts on NATO future.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who dismayed the three Baltic states by saying they were not yet ready for NATO, has reassured them in a letter that they are "fully eligible" for membership of the alliance.
Perry wrote to all the Baltic defence ministries. A copy of his letter to Lithuanian Defence Minister Linas Linkevicius was received by Lithuanian daily Lietuvos Rytas and made available to Reuters.
In it Perry said the United States firmly supported the security of the Baltic states and was committed to helping them integrate into Western structures, including NATO.

Last month he had shocked the Balts when he said at a defence ministers' meeting in Norway that Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia were not yet ready for NATO as they could not defend other NATO members.

It was the first open admission by a U.S. policy maker that the Balts were unlikely to be included in the planned early expansion of the alliance to take in former Communist-bloc countries. NATO diplomats, however, had been saying it quietly for some time.

The Baltic States, independent from the former Soviet Union since 1991, are anxious for strong security guarantees to make sure they never again come under the domination of Russia, which has ruled them for most of the last 200 years.

"I underscore that I said, and I believe, that the Balts are fully eligible for NATO membership and that I look forward to the day when each country is a member," Perry said in the letter, which was dated October 3.
The Lithuanian Defence Ministry said Perry's statement gave the Balts fresh hopes.
"The minister of defence is very positive about this letter. This is a stronger statement than the one we had in Norway," a Defence Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
In the letter, Perry said "some press reports and diplomatic chatter" had put an incorrect intepretation on his words in Norway.
He said media had focused on the negative aspect of his comments on the Balts' preparedness for the alliance, which he said were made in a "spirit of realism and practicality".
Perry said that, although the Balts were not ready at the moment, Washington would work with them to get their defence capability up to alliance standards.
"The U.S. has led in supporting the independence and security of the Baltic countries. The DoD (U.S. Department of Defence) and I share fully in that commitment," the letter said.
"I look forward to continuing work with you and the other Baltic ministers to help prepare your nations and defence establishments to assume the responsibilities of NATO membership," Perry added.
In a clear reference to Russia, Perry also reiterated that no country outside the alliance could veto the entry of another nation into NATO.
Russia, opposed to any NATO expansion but especially sensitive about the Balts, was cited by some diplomats as one of the main reasons for Western reluctance to admit them to NATO.

"In particular I reject -- and the U.S. rejects -- any idea that the Baltic countries are excluded a priori or that any non-NATO country has a veto over their aspirations -- whether de jure or de facto," Perry said.
Other Baltic officials said Perry's words were encouraging after the earlier apparent rebuff.
"This letter explains very well that this (Perry's) statement should not be taken as excluding the Baltic countries (from NATO)," an Estonian official told Reuters.
